title: TitleTitle: Charged $69 for a Spotify Account I Thought Was Free — Frustrating Customer Service
text: **Title: Spotify Charged Me for Months, Then Refused a $13.90 Refund — Terrible Customer Service**I discovered Spotify had been charging my credit card $13.90 per month despite my understanding that I had a free account. I checked both Apple and Google, neither of which showed an active paid subscription.On November 16, I contacted Spotify customer support to dispute the charges and request a refund.What followed was an unnecessarily frustrating experience. I was asked repeatedly for information I had already provided, including the transaction date, amount, email addresses, and screenshots of my credit card statement. I was also required to complete a secure credit card verification form that initially failed to open.Eventually, the representative located a Premium account associated with another email address. She explained that a three-month free trial began March 14, 2026, and that billing started June 14. I believe I had attempted to cancel before the trial ended, and I had not knowingly intended to maintain a paid subscription.By November, approximately $69 had been charged for a service I wasn't using.Despite explaining the situation and requesting a refund of just the most recent $13.90 charge, Spotify's representative stated that they could not refund the amount requested.What bothers me most is that I spent nearly an hour trying to resolve a $13.90 charge, only to encounter repeated requests for information, confusing account identification, and no satisfactory resolution.I wasn't asking for anything unreasonable. I wanted Spotify to acknowledge the confusion surrounding multiple accounts and refund a charge for a service I didn't intend to purchase.**Spotify was willing to collect approximately $69 in subscription payments but unwilling to refund even $13.90 when I raised the issue.**My advice: Check your credit card statements carefully, especially if you have ever signed up for a Spotify free trial. Having a Spotify Free account does not necessarily mean another account isn't being billed.Extremely disappointing billing experience and customer service. I expected better from a company of this size.

text: Extremely disappointing experience with Spotify Premium Family support.I have been a Spotify customer for several years and I manage a Premium Family plan allowing up to 6 members. My plan currently has only 4 members, yet Spotify is now preventing me from adding any new members.The issue was reported to Spotify Support on August 29, 30 and 31, 2026.Several different people have successively encountered the same restriction. In the most recent case, the invited member was rejected before even being given the opportunity to enter the household address.After numerous exchanges with Support, Spotify eventually informed me in writing that the restriction resulted from an “automatic risk detection” and later referred to an “automatic protection”.I repeatedly requested:– the precise reason for the restriction;– the date and event that triggered it;– the contractual rule involved;– how long the restriction will last;– the conditions required for it to be lifted;– and a genuine human review of the decision.I have received no precise answer to any of these questions.On August 30, one Spotify adviser wrote:“We unfortunately cannot lift this restriction.”When I asked for the official reason, the adviser replied:“The official reason is that I do not have any more information to provide you.”Yet only a few hours later, the same support service told me:“Don’t worry, your problem will be resolved.”Then, following another review, Spotify eventually stated:“This action is blocked by an automatic protection that we cannot disable.”This is precisely what I find unacceptable: contradictory answers, promises that the problem will be resolved followed by refusals, numerous changes of support advisers, and still no concrete explanation as to why my paid subscription is being restricted in this way.I have kept the emails, screenshots, names of advisers, dates and times of the conversations. title: Spotify's desktop app stopped producing audio, no support or refund
text: Spotify's desktop app stopped producing audio on my Mac while all other audio worked normally. I contacted support, where a bot (which refused to identify itself as such) declined a refund for a service that was not functioning, offered no compensation, and presented only two options: perform an indefinite amount of unpaid labor troubleshooting, or cancel moving forward. When I asked to speak with a human agent, I was denied. When I indicated I would send the chat transcript to the FTC and our state's AG office, I was transferred to a human agent. The human agent offered no meaningful support, including suggested a fix of reinstalling the app, did not work. The reinstall does not clear a hidden local config directory that was the actual source of the problem. I resolved the issue myself after ending the support session and spending considerable individual effort. If you have the same problem (desktop app silent, browser or other audio works fine), quit Spotify, open Terminal, run rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Spotify, and relaunch. You will need to log in again, but it resets the corrupted audio routing config that a normal reinstall leaves in place.A company that charges $23.53/month for a family plan should be able to diagnose its own software failures, not recite refund policy while its product sits broken.

title: Please fix the free version, Spotify.
text: The free version works fine for about five seconds until you try to loop songs. On the mobile app especially, songs on the free version cannot be looped properly. I've tried adding playlists with one song entered, over, and over, and over again. However, if you're like me, and you like listening to YOUR music, and not the recommended songs that Spotify forces on you, you're eventually going to run into the problem where it says, "Cannot queue this content." In fact, even if you go to the search bar and pick a song there, it will not play that song. It will play another "recommended song." That is not what a user wants! They want to listen to their music that they CHOOSE. Not a recommended song. I will say, giving some credit to Spotify here, adding a single song on a playlist does work in looping it. However, this is largely counteracted with Spotify mixing in recommended songs in that playlist due to "Smart Shuffle." Some people just want to loop their music without having to pay for a subscription.Another issue that I have found incredibly annoying are the "Made For You" playlists. Some people may find these just fine. Even I have a "Made For You" playlist that I listen to regularly. My only issue that I have with those playlists is the fact that you can't delete them. C'mon, at least let us users be able to have an option to remove these from our home screens so it's not cluttered up with 5 or 6 playlists we'll never listen too. At least for me, a lot of these playlists are single songs that I listened to because I accidentally hit a playlist instead of a song. I'll admit, yes that is my fault for not reading, but at least give us the option to remove unwanted playlists, even if they are made for us.Oh, and don't get me started with, what I like to call, "Undead Playlists." Once upon a time, a younger me made a playlist. I listened to it, enjoyed it, but music taste changes (something that I don't think Spotify really considers unless you're actively "removing from taste profile"), so now an older me tried deleting that playlist. And it deleted...for three seconds. I closed and reopened the app the next day, and what do you know? There it is, an empty playlist, taking up space, undelete-able. And I can't remove it to this day. This is something super annoying, ruining the user experience, that could be fixed with a simple feature of being able to remove unwanted playlists from your homepage!I want to be able to freely skip songs that I don't want to listen to, instead of just 6 an hour. I want to be able to listen to whatever song I want, when I want, however many times I choose to. I want to be able to clear unwanted playlists from my homepage. Above all, I want these features available on free version of the Spotify app. Users should NOT be forced to pay for a subscription just to have a good user experience. Lot of us don't have the option to pay for a subscription whatsoever. As far as I'm aware, the free trial doesn't even activate on the mobile app, at least, it doesn't for me.The only, only downside that the free version should be the adds. Whether a user is paying for a subscription, or a user is interrupted with adds, Spotify will make money either way.Fix the user experience for free users. Stop breaking the free version of Spotify just to get users to pay for a $12.99 subscription.I hope you consider this message, and have a wonderful day.

title: Spotify is a vGreat for listeners, frustrating for independent artistsery strong platform from…
text: Spotify is a very strong platform from a listener’s perspective: it is convenient, easy to use, offers a huge music library, and has become one of the main places where people discover and listen to music.From the perspective of an independent artist, however, my experience is much more disappointing. Spotify gives the impression of reach and visibility, but in practice very little of that turns into real support or sustainable growth. Streams generate extremely low income, older achievements quickly lose visibility, follower numbers feel unstable, and without additional marketing money almost nothing happens.The problem is not Spotify alone, but the whole system around it. Artists create the music, invest time, money and energy, while platforms, distributors, labels and marketing services benefit far more from the structure. For independent musicians, this can easily become frustrating: you keep working, hoping and investing, but the system rarely gives much back.For listeners, Spotify is excellent. For independent artists, it can be deeply discouraging, unfair and exhausting.

Instead, podcast episodes are still constantly interrupted by host-read sponsorships and promotional segments. Music playback is mostly excellent, but the podcast experience feels misleading when paying customers still have to manually skip through ads and sponsored interruptions. title: Spotify is just a money grabbing app
text: Spotify is an absolute masterclass in how to take a brilliant idea—instant access to millions of songs—and completely suffocate it under layers of incompetence, greed, and baffling design decisions.Let’s start with the free version, which isn’t so much a service as it is an endurance test. The ads aren’t just frequent—they’re relentless, repetitive, and somehow engineered to be as irritating as possible. It’s less “listen to music” and more “occasionally hear a song between audio torture sessions.” Whoever decided the ads should be louder than the music deserves a special place in UX hell.Then you upgrade, thinking you’re escaping the nightmare. You’re not. You’ve just paid to be mildly less annoyed. The so-called “premium” experience still manages to feel half-baked. Features break, downloads vanish, and the app behaves like it’s being held together by duct tape and wishful thinking.The interface? A chaotic, over-engineered disaster. It constantly rearranges itself like it’s ashamed of its own layout. Want to find a song you liked yesterday? Good luck. Spotify would rather shove 15 “curated” playlists down your throat than let you access your own music without a scavenger hunt. It’s like the app resents the idea that you might know what you want to listen to.And the recommendations—wow. Spotify loves to brag about its algorithm, but it seems to have the memory of a goldfish with a head injury. It cycles the same songs endlessly, pretending it’s “discovering” things for you when it’s really just stuck on repeat. It’s less personalized and more aggressively clueless.Performance-wise, it’s a mess. Random pauses, songs skipping, the app freezing at the worst possible moments—it’s like every update is a gamble to see what new problem they can introduce. Offline mode is especially laughable, as if the app forgets its entire purpose the second your signal drops.At this point, Spotify doesn’t feel like a music platform—it feels like a bloated, self-important middleman that actively makes music harder to enjoy. It’s impressive, in the worst possible way, how consistently it manages to get in its own way.If there were an award for turning something simple into something unbearable, Spotify wouldn’t just win—it would curate a playlist about it and still somehow mess that up.

text: I must confess, I’ve encountered few services as utterly incompetent as Spotify’s approach to customer care. Yes, you read that correctly. Because apparently, if my profile reflects my current country of residence, and my card is issued elsewhere, the very notion of logic is discarded. One wonders: am I now required to maintain a fleet of local credit cards around the globe just to pay for what should be a seamless digital service?Spotify, let me be crystal clear. The issue is not my card. It is your inability to reconcile a user’s profile with a reality that exists outside your narrow, myopic system. I expected elegance, efficiency, discretion — what I received was amateurism, frustration, and the maddening sensation that I am negotiating with a particularly dim-witted bureaucracy.If you value your time, your patience, or your dignity, tread carefully. title: Should be called Greedify
text: I’ve been a loyal Spotify Premium subscriber since around 2019, and over the years I’ve spent close to $900 on this platform. Until now, I’ve genuinely enjoyed using it — but this recent decision to raise the subscription price to $16 a month is honestly infuriating and disappointing.There have been no meaningful improvements or new features to justify this increase. Spotify keeps mentioning “innovation” and “investment in customer experience,” but as someone who’s been paying for six years, I’ve seen no real evidence of that. The app functions pretty much the same — ad-free music and playlists. If ad-free listening is still the only real benefit, then charging $16 a month feels like pure greed, not innovation.Spotify claims to offer “plans tailored to different needs,” but these mainly benefit students, couples, and families. What about single users, retirees, or low-income individuals who don’t qualify for those discounts? The lack of fair or flexible options for these groups feels exclusionary, especially at a time when the cost of living is rising globally.What frustrates me most is the templated responses from customer support. I understand they have to follow protocol, but nothing in their message addressed the real question — what exactly are we paying more for? If there’s no visible improvement, it’s impossible to justify a higher price tag.I’ve supported Spotify for years because I believed in the service, but this latest move shows a lack of respect for long-term subscribers. It’s disappointing to see a company so focused on profit over people. I will no longer be paying for this service!Shame on Spotify for forgetting the loyalty of its users.

title: Losing a premium user due to how you treat your free users.
text: Having been a Spotify Premium user for 3-4 years now, I am unable to renew my subscription due to current financial constraints. I figured I'd use the free--with ads-- version for a while until I can renew. That said, I am so disappointed by the amount of ads you are forced to listen to that it's not even worth it. There's a good chance I won't renew with Spotify because I'm ready to find a new service after only five days of free listening. To show what I'm talking about, here is an hour worth of listening and how many ads I had to endure in that time. If you consider that the total amount of ads was 9 minutes out of 65 minutes, that means that ~15% of what you listen to is ads. While that isn't a disproportionately large amount (compared to old-school TV stations which were often 25% ads), the problem is it is impossible to get into your music when you are interrupted every couple songs by loud ads. Some of the ad sets were no more than 6.5 minutes apart. As a result you only get to hear 2-3 songs between 1.5 minute ad sets. This is particularly unbearable for someone like me who likes to listen to music at high volume, just to be blasted with obnoxiously loud ads after every 2nd or 3rd song.12:03   - 4 ads 1.5m (ended at 12:04.5)12:12.5 - 3 ads 1.5m (ended at 12:14)12:20.5 - 2 ads 1.5m (ended at 12:22)	-- One song automatically skipped after 30 seconds and next ads came even sooner at 6.5 minutes12:29.5 - 3 ads 1.5m (ended at 12:31)12:39.75 - 3 ads 1.5m (ended at 12.41.25)	-- Long 5s+ pause between multiple songs for no reason on this set12:53.75 - 3 ads 1.75m (ended at 12:55.5)01:07.5 - 3 ads 1.25m (ended at 01:08.75)This is abrasive and abusive towards your free users. You could easily do longer ad sets with longer ad-free listening in between so that people can actually turn up their favorite music and enjoy it without being jolted with anxiety every 7.5 minutes when an obnoxious ad blasts over the speakers.Furthermore, I noticed a couple other things that have degraded my opinion of Spotify.1) A song automatically skipped a few seconds inn. While this happens occasionally even with Premium, this time I was made to listen to ads even sooner, after a mere 6.5 minutes, despite that I'm not the one who skipped the song.2) During one set there were multiple long pauses between songs for no reason. I have 300MB download speed, and this never happened with Premium, so I know it wasn't on my end. This leads me to believe that these random 5 second pauses are just to pad your listening and decrease costs while keeping the same amount of ad revenue between songs sets.3) When my premium first expired I was getting 10-20 minutes between ad sets. The longer I have listened without premium, the less actual music I get to listen to. In only five days, 10-20 minutes has degraded to less than 9 on average. Like an intentional manipulation to push the user towards buying premium (and if they don't, you don't care because they're obviously willing to accept garbage if they keep using the service for free).4) Pausing the music seems to be a bad idea, and it seems like every time I return, the one song finishes out and then I have to listen to another ad set--even if that was the first song after the last ad set. This is unnecessary and probably the most abusive part of all of this. If I haven't been listening, I shouldn't have to "earn" more free listening by listening to a second set of ads. This is a common tactic I see in streaming platforms these days. Hulu being the worst I've seen, where they intentionally set your show or movie back up to 10 minutes to try and put you behind an ad set you already watched. Yet if you are watching an ad free movie, it never sets you back at all. Blatant abuse.

text: Facial recognition for a music app is not just unnecessary — it’s a security risk.As someone in cybersecurity, I can tell you: biometric data is not like a password. You can’t change your face when it gets breached. Storing or even processing facial data creates a massive attack surface for hackers and data brokers — and Spotify doesn’t have a clean enough record to justify this level of invasive tech.This isn’t banking or healthcare. It’s music. There is no reason for a streaming service to request biometric scans. Once this data exists, it’s a target — and the user has zero control over how it’s stored, shared, or potentially sold.Facial recognition is already notorious for bias, misidentification, and abuse. For Spotify to normalize this in the entertainment space is a terrifying precedent.If this isn’t immediately walked back, I’ll be canceling my subscription and advising everyone — clients, friends, and colleagues — to do the same. Your playlist is not worth your privacy.

title: Quite good, but a lot of issues need fixing still
text: I feel like we’re giving Spotify a hard time on here for things that aren’t entirely fair, or at least not that relevant. The main argument for Spotify, which is what puts it over it’s competitors like Tidal, Apple Music and Deezer, is simply it’s algorithm. If there is one thing they do well, it is putting people onto good music, and in my opinion, that is one of the main tasks a service like Spotify needs to accomplish. That being said, there are a few very good reasons, especially with recent adjustments, that bitter the taste a bit. One thing, that I as a musician myself have to point out immediately, is the fact that they pay the artists very poorly. About half of what Apple Music pays per stream. I also feel like it should be quite possible for Spotify to compete with the likes of Tidal in high quality audio, which is one of Tidal’s key advantages. Political correctness, in censoring Rechts-Rock, could also be taken a bit more seriously, as Deezer is showing off. The new day-lists are a very good addition in my opinion, however I would prefer if the algorithm would still favor music of artists I already enjoy and listen to regularly on the main page, rather than highest selling releases, regardless of genre and likeness to my taste. Also, please make the new music tab more quickly accessible again. You had that down previously, why did you change it? All in all, I’m sitting somewhere around a 3,5. As of now, I’m willing to lean towards 4, but I’m unsure how long these factors can be left untreated until that changes. One competitor adjusting it’s algorithm, could be all it takes before people really start leaving, and it feels like they aren’t aware enough of that.

But before I could even do anything, my music was already deleted. (This is because I was on vacation and didn't keep an eye on my songs for a few weeks).In my opinion Spotify is responsible for this. They need to punish the guy who makes these weird playlists. Not the artist who didn't ask/pay for it. It is sad that the opposite of the law applies here. Guilty until proven innocent. I speak on behalf of many artists who have the same problem. I pay a lot of money to have 1 song online. 300+ euro. You think I'll risk all this for just 2k (fake) streams? While I have already achieved 10k+ organically on 1 song? It's time to work on this! Now you can punish every small artist by throwing/having fake streams thrown on there song(s). And it just gets deleted. Spotify i know its frustrating that people pay for fake streams. text: Certainly! Here's a comprehensive review highlighting the key features and benefits of Spotify:"Spotify is an unparalleled music streaming platform that has revolutionized the way we listen to music. Its vast library of over millions of songs across various genres, languages, and cultures caters to the diverse musical tastes of its users worldwide.One of Spotify's standout features is its user-friendly interface, which offers seamless navigation through playlists, albums, and personalized recommendations. The 'Discover Weekly' and 'Release Radar' playlists intelligently curate music based on individual listening habits, introducing users to new artists and tracks they might love.The platform's algorithm-driven recommendations, coupled with its robust search functionality, empower users to effortlessly explore and discover music tailored to their preferences. Additionally, the collaborative playlist feature fosters social engagement, allowing friends to create and contribute to shared playlists, enhancing the communal aspect of music discovery.Spotify's subscription tiers offer flexibility, with a free ad-supported version and premium plans that unlock ad-free listening, offline downloads, higher audio quality, and unlimited skips. Its compatibility across multiple devices, including smartphones, tablets, desktops, and smart speakers, ensures music is accessible anytime, anywhere.The platform's commitment to supporting artists through initiatives like 'Spotify for Artists' and features like 'Canvas' (which allows artists to personalize their tracks with looping visuals) demonstrates its dedication to promoting and empowering musicians.Furthermore, Spotify's podcasts and audio content add depth to its offerings, featuring a wide range of topics, from educational series to entertaining discussions, making it a one-stop destination for both music and spoken-word content.In conclusion, Spotify sets the gold standard for music streaming services, combining an extensive music library, intuitive interface, personalized recommendations, and support for artists. Its continuous innovation and commitment to enhancing the music streaming experience solidify its position as a leader in the industry, catering to the evolving needs of music enthusiasts worldwide."

title: Listening to music on Spotify is an…
text: Listening to music on Spotify is an incredibly enjoyable experience. The platform boasts an extensive library of songs, spanning across various genres, artists, and eras. Whether you're into pop, rock, hip-hop, or classical, there's something for everyone.One of the most impressive features of Spotify is its ability to personalize recommendations based on your listening history. The more you use the platform, the more it learns about your preferences, and the better it becomes at suggesting new music that you're likely to enjoy. This means you can discover new artists and songs effortlessly, without having to search for them manually.Spotify's user interface is sleek, intuitive, and easy to navigate, making it simple to find the music you want to listen to. Why I gave three stars and not five: - I used to pay for a Family package, and now the Duo package. On both packages I've been unable to successfully add people to my premium even though they're all under one roof and follow the instructions. I'm not very proactive with this stuff, so I've likely lost out on a few £££ because only I can access the premium non-ad service compared to the rest of my family that I HAVE tried to add and pay for. - Quality of service. I feel like talking to real people who truly care is not possible. I work my way through the community site, trailing through page after page, only to find ad hoc answers that don't actually work. Whilst I appreciate you must have subscribers into the millions, other companies do and they still provide an online chat service to assist. Why can't Spotify? I've used other services, and to be honest, I wouldn't want to use any other service. Spotify is so easy to use as a premium, single user and has such a large library! My only recommendation is to please assist people who are paying more for duo or family services to actually receive the service they're paying for. I'm beginning to believe Spotify doesn't care about the people giving their company millions of £££.
